Abolished
a-bŏl´ĭsht
v. (annulled, done away; rendering Greek katargeo)
From Latin abolere, to destroy. The Greek katargeo means to render inoperative — to leave a thing in place while stripping its power.

Biblical Definition

To be abolished is to be annulled. Paul says Christ “hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2Ti 1:10). Ephesians says He abolished “in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” to make one new man of two (Eph 2:15). And of the fading glory on Moses' face, Paul says the children of Israel could not look to the end of “that which is abolished” (2Co 3:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines abolish as to make void; to annul; to abrogate; and to destroy, or put an end to.

expand to see more

ABOLISH, v.t. To make void; to annul; to abrogate; applied chiefly and appropriately to established laws, contracts, rites, customs and institutions.

2. To destroy, or put an end to; as to abolish idols.

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:10 — "But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:"

Eph 2:15 — "Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;"

2Co 3:13 — "And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished:"

1Co 15:26 — "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death."

Modern Corruption

Death is still described by Christians as the end, and Paul says it has been abolished — left standing as an experience while stripped of its power.

expand to see more

2 Timothy 1:10 makes a claim that sounds false to observation: Christ hath abolished death. People plainly still die. The Greek helps — katargeo is to render inoperative rather than to remove, and the second half of the verse supplies the mechanism: and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. Death remains an event and has ceased to be a destination. Paul says elsewhere that the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, so the abolition is real and its final execution is scheduled.

Ephesians 2:15 uses the same verb of the ceremonial barrier: having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace. The purpose clause matters. The abolition was not an act of dismissal toward the law but the means of forming one people out of two, which is what the whole chapter is about.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, abolish; the same verb for charity never faileth and for the law's ordinances.

expand to see more

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle, abolish; 2 Timothy 1:10, Ephesians 2:15, 2 Corinthians 3:7-14, 1 Corinthians 13:8.

Greek aphtharsia (G861) — immortality, incorruption; 2 Timothy 1:10.

Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity; Ephesians 2:15-16, abolished in his flesh.

Usage

"“Hath abolished death, and hath brought life… to light” — an event, no longer a destination."

"“Abolished in his flesh the enmity” — the means of making one new man."

"“That which is abolished” — the fading glory Moses veiled."
